title: Clarifying a vague concern
stem: A client awaiting biopsy results says, 'I cannot deal with what comes next.' What response best clarifies the concern?
options: 'Which part of what comes next feels hardest right now?'
'Most biopsies turn out well.'
'Try to concentrate on today's meals.'
'Your family will manage the decisions.'
why: An open focused question invites the client's actual meaning.
Reassurance assumes an outcome and may close discussion.
Redirection bypasses the expressed concern.
Family involvement does not replace understanding the client's needs.
takeaway: Clarify the client's meaning before offering reassurance or solutions.
learningObjective: Clarify the client's meaning before offering reassurance or solutions.

title: Observing inconsistent cues
stem: A client says the upcoming operation is 'fine' while trembling and avoiding discussion. What should the nurse say?
options: 'You should not be frightened.'
'I notice your hands shaking; how are you feeling about tomorrow?'
'Your consent form shows you are comfortable.'
'We can discuss it after surgery.'
why: Telling the client how to feel discourages disclosure.
A neutral observation invites clarification without assuming emotion.
Consent does not establish absence of anxiety.
Delay misses a current opportunity for support.
takeaway: Explore discrepancies between verbal and nonverbal communication.
learningObjective: Explore discrepancies between verbal and nonverbal communication.

title: Responding to anger about waiting
stem: A client says, 'No one cares; I have waited all morning.' No threats are present. What is the best response?
options: Defend each staffing decision
Explain that other clients are more important
Acknowledge frustration and clarify the immediate need
Ask the client to complain only in writing
why: Defensiveness may intensify the sense of not being heard.
Ranking personal importance is invalidating.
Acknowledgment and assessment can identify a practical response.
A written process does not replace addressing current needs.
takeaway: Acknowledge frustration before clarifying what assistance is needed.
learningObjective: Acknowledge frustration before clarifying what assistance is needed.

title: Avoiding premature advice
stem: A client is deciding whether to tell an adult child about a diagnosis and asks, 'What would you do?' What is most therapeutic?
options: Describe the nurse's family experience at length
Tell the client disclosure is always best
Ask the adult child to decide
Explore the client's concerns and possible outcomes of each choice
why: Extended self-disclosure shifts attention away from the client.
A universal instruction ignores the relationship and preferences.
The decision belongs to the capable client.
Exploring choices supports the client's own informed decision.
takeaway: Support decision-making without substituting the nurse's personal choice.
learningObjective: Support decision-making without substituting the nurse's personal choice.

title: Checking shared understanding
stem: Which communication practices reduce misunderstandings during a sensitive interview? Select all that apply.
options: Summarize key points and invite correction
Clarify unfamiliar expressions
Interpret silence as agreement
Complete the client's sentences whenever speech slows
why: Summaries reveal whether the nurse has understood accurately.
Clarification avoids assigning an unintended meaning.
Silence can reflect many emotions or communication needs.
Interrupting may alter meaning and discourage expression.
takeaway: Verify meaning rather than assuming shared understanding.
learningObjective: Verify meaning rather than assuming shared understanding.

title: A client declines conversation
stem: A client newly diagnosed with cancer says, 'I do not want to talk now.' They show no immediate safety concern. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue questioning to prevent avoidance
Respect the request and agree how to reconnect later
Ask relatives to persuade the client immediately
Document refusal of all psychosocial support
why: Continued pressure can undermine trust.
Respect and a planned return preserve access to support.
Immediate persuasion may disregard the client's expressed boundary.
Declining now does not mean rejecting future support.
takeaway: Respect temporary limits while keeping support available.
learningObjective: Respect temporary limits while keeping support available.

title: Supporting slowed responses
stem: A client with depression takes a long time to answer questions but remains engaged. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask several questions rapidly
Answer for the client
Allow time and use one clear question at a time
End the interview because participation is impossible
why: Rapid questioning can overwhelm slowed processing.
Supplying answers prevents an accurate client account.
Time and simple pacing support meaningful participation.
Slow responses do not establish inability to engage.
takeaway: Adapt interview pace to the client's processing speed.
learningObjective: Adapt interview pace to the client's processing speed.

title: Naming emotion tentatively
stem: After discussing job loss, a client looks away and clenches their hands. Which response best checks emotion without assuming it?
options: 'You seem upset; what is happening for you?'
'You are clearly angry at your employer.'
'At least you have more free time.'
'You should start job searching today.'
why: Tentative observation allows the client to confirm or correct meaning.
A fixed interpretation may mislabel the emotion.
Positive reframing may minimize a painful loss.
Immediate advice bypasses assessment of current needs.
takeaway: Offer tentative observations and invite the client's interpretation.
learningObjective: Offer tentative observations and invite the client's interpretation.

title: Maintaining therapeutic focus
stem: A client asks detailed questions about the nurse's divorce during a discussion of their own separation. What is the best response?
options: Share the full story to establish equality
Refuse abruptly and leave
Compare whose separation was harder
Briefly redirect toward what the client needs from this conversation
why: Extensive disclosure can shift care toward the nurse's needs.
Abrupt withdrawal can damage rapport unnecessarily.
Comparison invalidates individual experience.
A respectful boundary keeps the discussion useful to the client.
takeaway: Limit self-disclosure to preserve the therapeutic focus.
learningObjective: Limit self-disclosure to preserve the therapeutic focus.

title: Communicating through an interpreter
stem: During a mental-health interview, which practices support the client's participation? Select all that apply.
options: Address the client directly
Allow extra time for interpretation
Ask a child relative to interpret trauma details
Clarify confidentiality and the interpreter's role
why: Direct engagement maintains the therapeutic relationship.
Interpretation needs time for accuracy and emotional processing.
A child may lack skills and face inappropriate emotional burden.
Role clarity supports trust and informed participation.
takeaway: Use qualified interpretation with clear roles during sensitive interviews.
learningObjective: Use qualified interpretation with clear roles during sensitive interviews.

title: Ending a therapeutic meeting
stem: A client becomes distressed when the nurse abruptly announces the session is over. What change would best improve future meetings?
options: Avoid discussing endings until the last moment
Give advance notice and summarize a plan for next contact
Extend every meeting indefinitely
Ask another client to provide reassurance
why: Unexpected endings may increase uncertainty or abandonment concerns.
Predictable closure supports continuity and emotional preparation.
Indefinite extension is not a sustainable therapeutic boundary.
Other clients should not be assigned this support role.
takeaway: Prepare clients for endings and clarify the next contact.
learningObjective: Prepare clients for endings and clarify the next contact.

title: A repeated request for reassurance
stem: A client repeatedly asks whether staff are annoyed with them despite prior reassurance. What response best explores the pattern?
options: Repeat reassurance without discussion each time
Tell the client to stop asking
Ask what happens just before the worry returns
Avoid the client to reduce reinforcement
why: Reassurance alone may not reveal the trigger or need.
Dismissal may intensify insecurity.
Trigger exploration can identify concerns and useful coping strategies.
Avoidance can worsen mistrust and distress.
takeaway: Explore triggers when reassurance does not provide lasting relief.
learningObjective: Explore triggers when reassurance does not provide lasting relief.

title: Validating without agreeing
stem: A client feels betrayed because a sibling cannot visit and says, 'They never cared about me.' What is the best response?
options: 'It sounds painful to feel unsupported today.'
'Your sibling is selfish.'
'You know they care, so stop saying that.'
'Other clients have no visitors at all.'
why: Naming the pain validates emotion without judging the sibling.
Agreement confirms an unassessed interpretation.
Contradiction may close discussion of the client's experience.
Comparison minimizes the individual's distress.
takeaway: Validate feelings without endorsing unverified conclusions.
learningObjective: Validate feelings without endorsing unverified conclusions.

title: Exploring strengths in crisis
stem: A client overwhelmed by a housing problem says, 'Nothing I do works.' What question best supports assessment of coping strengths?
options: 'Why did you let this happen?'
'Can your family solve everything for you?'
'Would you rather avoid the issue?'
'What has helped you get through difficult situations before?'
why: Blame discourages useful assessment.
Family resources should be assessed without assuming complete dependence.
Avoidance does not identify existing strengths.
Previous effective coping may offer practical resources for this crisis.
takeaway: Identify previous coping strengths when a client feels powerless.
learningObjective: Identify previous coping strengths when a client feels powerless.

title: Repairing a communication error
stem: Which actions are appropriate after a nurse realizes they misunderstood a client's statement? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledge the misunderstanding
Ask the client to clarify the intended meaning
Continue with the original interpretation to avoid embarrassment
Reflect the corrected understanding back to the client
why: Acknowledgment supports honesty and trust.
Clarification centres the client's own meaning.
Persisting with an error risks inappropriate care.
Reflection checks that the correction is accurate.
takeaway: Repair misunderstandings openly and verify the corrected meaning.
learningObjective: Repair misunderstandings openly and verify the corrected meaning.

title: Anxiety before a procedure
stem: A client awaiting a procedure can discuss worries but repeatedly asks what will happen. What intervention fits this level of anxiety?
options: Provide clear short explanations and invite questions
Delay all information until sedation begins
Give a lengthy technical lecture without pauses
Assume medication is the only useful support
why: The client can process focused information and clarification.
Delaying removes an opportunity for informed preparation.
Excess detail may increase rather than reduce overload.
Communication and coping support remain useful interventions.
takeaway: Match information complexity to the client's ability to process anxiety.
learningObjective: Match information complexity to the client's ability to process anxiety.

title: Unexpected chest symptoms
stem: A client with a history of panic reports new chest pressure and sweating. What should the nurse do first?
options: Attribute symptoms to the known anxiety disorder
Assess urgently for physical causes while providing calm support
Begin a prolonged exploration of childhood stress
Advise waiting until the next therapy appointment
why: A psychiatric history does not exclude an acute physical illness.
New symptoms require appropriate physical assessment and timely escalation.
Detailed exploration delays assessment of possible acute illness.
Delayed follow-up is inappropriate for this new presentation.
takeaway: Assess new physical symptoms without diagnostic overshadowing.
learningObjective: Assess new physical symptoms without diagnostic overshadowing.

title: After a panic episode
stem: A client's acute panic has settled and they can focus. What is the most useful next step?
options: Analyse triggers during another acute episode only
Encourage avoiding every associated situation permanently
Review early cues and practise an agreed coping response
Assume improvement means no further support is needed
why: Learning is more feasible after intense distress subsides.
Broad avoidance may reinforce anxiety and limit function.
Reflection and rehearsal support earlier response to future symptoms.
Temporary relief does not establish a sustainable coping plan.
takeaway: Review panic triggers and coping after the client regains focus.
learningObjective: Review panic triggers and coping after the client regains focus.

title: Generalized worry and function
stem: A client worries about many everyday matters and now misses work because of poor sleep. What should the nurse assess beyond worry content?
options: Functional effects, coping, substances and safety
Only whether each worry is objectively likely
Whether the client can suppress thoughts on command
Which family member is most optimistic
why: Broader assessment identifies severity, contributors and support needs.
Probability debate alone does not assess impairment or risk.
Voluntary suppression is not a sufficient clinical assessment.
Another person's optimism does not describe the client's functioning.
takeaway: Assess how anxiety affects function and what sustains it.
learningObjective: Assess how anxiety affects function and what sustains it.

title: Preparing for graded exposure
stem: A client receiving therapy for a specific phobia has agreed to a graded plan. What nursing action best supports it?
options: Introduce the most feared situation without warning
Remove every exposure opportunity indefinitely
Change the hierarchy independently each shift
Reinforce the agreed small step and review the client's response
why: Unexpected intense exposure undermines collaboration and may overwhelm coping.
Complete avoidance conflicts with the agreed therapeutic plan.
Uncoordinated changes reduce consistency and predictability.
Planned manageable practice supports treatment and evaluation.
takeaway: Support agreed gradual exposure without improvising coercive challenges.
learningObjective: Support agreed gradual exposure without improvising coercive challenges.

title: Anxiety coping skills
stem: Which strategies can a nurse practise with a willing client when anxiety is manageable? Select all that apply.
options: A grounding exercise focused on current surroundings
A paced breathing technique the client finds comfortable
Repeatedly reviewing catastrophic possibilities as reassurance
Identifying a supportive contact and early warning cues
why: Present-focused attention can reduce overwhelming internal focus.
Comfortable paced breathing can support regulation.
Repeated catastrophic review can reinforce worry rather than coping.
Early cues and support improve timely use of the plan.
takeaway: Practise coping skills when the client can engage and learn.
learningObjective: Practise coping skills when the client can engage and learn.

title: Social anxiety and participation
stem: A client wants to join a group but fears speaking in front of everyone. What plan best supports participation?
options: Require leading the next group
Agree on a manageable first role with the client and therapist
Exclude the client from all groups
Ask the group to challenge the fear publicly
why: Sudden intense demands may overwhelm the client.
A graded collaborative role supports valued participation.
Exclusion reinforces avoidance and removes opportunity.
Public confrontation may increase shame and distress.
takeaway: Support gradual chosen participation for social anxiety.
learningObjective: Support gradual chosen participation for social anxiety.

title: Caffeine and anxiety patterns
stem: A client reports evening palpitations after consuming several energy drinks during study sessions. They are currently stable. What should the nurse explore?
options: Only family psychiatric history
Whether drinks are sugar-free
Timing, quantity and relationship between stimulant use and symptoms
Whether classmates use the same brand
why: Family history does not assess the stated immediate pattern.
Sugar content does not identify stimulant exposure.
Pattern assessment can reveal a modifiable contributor while guiding evaluation.
Peer use does not establish the client's response.
takeaway: Assess stimulant exposure when evaluating anxiety-like symptoms.
learningObjective: Assess stimulant exposure when evaluating anxiety-like symptoms.

title: Anxiety versus immediate learning
stem: A highly anxious client cannot retain discharge instructions despite repeated teaching. What should the nurse do?
options: Address anxiety and readiness before retrying essential teaching
Increase the number of facts covered each minute
Ask for a signature as evidence of understanding
Send the same instructions without reassessment
why: Reducing distress can improve ability to process essential information.
More information may worsen cognitive overload.
A signature does not demonstrate learning.
Unchanged delivery may leave the safety gap unresolved.
takeaway: Restore readiness when anxiety prevents learning.
learningObjective: Restore readiness when anxiety prevents learning.

title: Evaluating anxiety improvement
stem: A client previously avoided all shopping because of anxiety. Which outcome best indicates meaningful improvement?
options: The client reports never feeling any anxiety
The client memorizes diagnostic terminology
The client stops discussing worry with staff
The client completes a planned short shopping trip using coping skills
why: Complete absence of anxiety is not required for improved function.
Vocabulary does not demonstrate coping or participation.
Reduced disclosure may conceal distress rather than show recovery.
Valued activity with coping reflects functional progress.
takeaway: Evaluate anxiety care through improved function and coping.
learningObjective: Evaluate anxiety care through improved function and coping.

title: Reassurance in health anxiety
stem: A client repeatedly seeks the same reassurance after appropriate assessment. Which approach supports a coordinated plan? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on planned review and symptom-reporting boundaries
Explore distress and coping without promising absolute certainty
Offer a new unplanned test every time worry returns
Ensure genuinely new concerning symptoms receive assessment
why: Consistency can reduce fragmented reassurance-seeking while preserving care.
Emotional support does not require impossible guarantees.
Repeated unplanned testing can reinforce the cycle without addressing distress.
A known anxiety pattern must not exclude new clinical evaluation.
takeaway: Balance consistent health-anxiety care with assessment of new symptoms.
learningObjective: Balance consistent health-anxiety care with assessment of new symptoms.

title: Obsessions and compulsions
stem: A client describes unwanted contamination thoughts and repeated washing that delays meals. What should the nurse focus on?
options: Whether the client knows more cleaning techniques
Distress, interference with function and the existing treatment plan
Proving that all surfaces are completely germ-free
Asking relatives to confirm the ritual is sensible
why: More cleaning methods may strengthen rather than assess the ritual.
Functional impact and treatment context guide appropriate support.
Absolute contamination certainty is unrealistic and can sustain reassurance cycles.
Agreement with rituals does not address impairment.
takeaway: Assess distress and functional interference from obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
learningObjective: Assess distress and functional interference from obsessive-compulsive symptoms.

title: An interrupted ritual
stem: A client with obsessive-compulsive disorder becomes distressed when a routine changes. No immediate danger is present. What is the best initial response?
options: Physically prevent all rituals without a plan
Insist the client explain why the fear is irrational
Acknowledge distress and use the agreed treatment strategies
Participate fully in the ritual until anxiety disappears
why: Abrupt unplanned interruption may escalate distress without therapeutic structure.
Arguing about rationality may not reduce the anxiety.
Consistent agreed strategies support coping and avoid improvisation.
Staff participation can reinforce compulsive behaviour.
takeaway: Respond to ritual-related distress through the coordinated treatment plan.
learningObjective: Respond to ritual-related distress through the coordinated treatment plan.

title: Family accommodation of rituals
stem: A family spends hours checking locks at a client's request. They ask how to help. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Discuss a gradual coordinated reduction in accommodation with the treatment team
Stop every supportive interaction immediately
Continue checking whenever requested as the main treatment
Debate each feared event until the client concedes
why: Planned changes can reduce reinforcement while supporting distress management.
Withdrawal of all support is broader than reducing ritual participation.
Repeated accommodation may maintain the compulsive cycle.
Lengthy debate can become another reassurance ritual.
takeaway: Coordinate family responses that reduce ritual accommodation without abandoning support.
learningObjective: Coordinate family responses that reduce ritual accommodation without abandoning support.

title: Evaluating OCD treatment progress
stem: Which finding best indicates useful progress for a client receiving treatment for compulsive checking?
options: A stronger ability to explain every feared catastrophe
More family members helping complete checks
No mention of rituals during one interview
Less time checking and improved ability to leave home as planned
why: Detailed fear descriptions do not establish reduced impairment.
Additional accommodation may maintain the problem.
Nondisclosure does not reliably indicate improvement.
Reduced interference and better function reflect meaningful treatment response.
takeaway: Evaluate obsessive-compulsive care by distress, ritual time and function.
learningObjective: Evaluate obsessive-compulsive care by distress, ritual time and function.

title: Supporting planned response prevention
stem: A client practising therapist-directed response prevention feels anxious after delaying a ritual. Which nursing actions fit the agreed plan? Select all that apply.
options: Stay supportive while the client uses coping skills
Record response and share it with the treatment team
Complete the ritual for the client
Remind the client of the agreed step without coercion
why: Support helps tolerate distress without automatically reinforcing the ritual.
Observations inform adjustment of the coordinated plan.
Staff completion defeats the purpose of response prevention.
Predictable collaborative guidance supports the treatment agreement.
takeaway: Support planned response prevention without completing the compulsion.
learningObjective: Support planned response prevention without completing the compulsion.

title: Compulsive behaviour and skin injury
stem: A client washes until their hands bleed but fears stopping. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Ignore the skin because the cause is psychological
Assess and treat the injury while coordinating support for the compulsion
Restrict every hygiene activity indefinitely
Focus solely on replacing the soap brand
why: Physical injury requires care regardless of its behavioural cause.
Both tissue damage and the driving distress need attention.
Broad restriction is not an individualized therapeutic plan.
Product change alone does not address repeated injurious washing.
takeaway: Address physical consequences and psychological drivers of compulsive behaviour.
learningObjective: Address physical consequences and psychological drivers of compulsive behaviour.

title: Hoarding and engagement
stem: A client is distressed by suggestions to discard possessions that obstruct home pathways. What approach best begins a therapeutic plan?
options: Arrange disposal without discussing consent or goals
Describe the possessions as worthless
Explore the client's meaning and agree on an immediate safety priority
Set complete clearance as the only acceptable first goal
why: Unilateral disposal may damage trust and intensify distress.
Dismissive language does not support engagement.
Understanding meaning and a shared safety goal support collaboration.
An overwhelming goal may prevent meaningful initial progress.
takeaway: Begin hoarding-related care with collaboration and specific safety priorities.
learningObjective: Begin hoarding-related care with collaboration and specific safety priorities.

title: Unwanted intrusive thoughts
stem: A client is ashamed of unwanted upsetting thoughts and says they conflict with personal values. What should the nurse do?
options: Explore the thoughts, distress, intent and safety without assuming desire to act
Conclude that any intrusive thought proves intent
Avoid the subject to reduce embarrassment
Promise absolute secrecy before assessment
why: Assessment distinguishes unwanted thoughts from intent while addressing safety.
Intrusive thoughts and intended actions are not equivalent.
Avoidance prevents accurate understanding and support.
Confidentiality has limits when safety requires intervention.
takeaway: Assess intrusive thoughts without equating them automatically with intent.
learningObjective: Assess intrusive thoughts without equating them automatically with intent.

title: Unexpected touch during care
stem: During a nonurgent assessment, a trauma survivor startles and says, 'Do not touch me.' What should the nurse do?
options: Complete the examination quickly
Explain that touch is required and continue
Ask the client to recount the trauma immediately
Stop, restore choice and discuss how to proceed
why: Speed does not replace consent or address distress.
Clinical purpose does not remove the need to respond to refusal.
Detailed recounting is not needed to restore immediate safety.
Pausing and renegotiating supports control and trust.
takeaway: Stop unwanted touch and re-establish choice during trauma-informed care.
learningObjective: Stop unwanted touch and re-establish choice during trauma-informed care.

title: Trauma-informed planning
stem: Which options may help a client who becomes distressed during examinations? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on a stop signal
Explain each step before contact
Require a complete trauma narrative before offering accommodations
Offer choices about positioning or a support person where feasible
why: A stop signal gives the client a clear way to regain control.
Predictability reduces unexpected sensations and actions.
Accommodations do not require detailed disclosure of trauma.
Feasible choices can increase safety and participation.
takeaway: Offer predictability and choice without requiring trauma disclosure.
learningObjective: Offer predictability and choice without requiring trauma disclosure.

title: Grounding during a flashback
stem: A client suddenly crouches behind a chair and says they are back at a past assault scene. There is no current physical threat. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask for a detailed chronological account
Calmly identify the present setting and invite attention to current surroundings
Approach rapidly from behind
Challenge the memory's factual accuracy
why: Detailed retelling can intensify current distress.
Present-focused grounding can support orientation and perceived safety.
Unexpected approach may increase the sense of threat.
Factual debate does not address the immediate experience.
takeaway: Use calm present-focused grounding during trauma re-experiencing.
learningObjective: Use calm present-focused grounding during trauma re-experiencing.

title: Nightmares and daytime function
stem: A trauma survivor reports nightmares, poor sleep and difficulty attending appointments. What should the nurse assess?
options: Only whether the trauma occurred recently
Whether the client can stop dreaming voluntarily
Sleep impact, current safety, coping and treatment supports
Whether relatives have more severe experiences
why: Trauma-related effects can persist beyond the recent period.
Dreams are not simply controlled by instruction.
Assessment should identify impairment, risk and available supports.
Comparing severity does not clarify this client's needs.
takeaway: Assess the functional and safety effects of trauma-related sleep disturbance.
learningObjective: Assess the functional and safety effects of trauma-related sleep disturbance.

title: Disclosure without pressure
stem: A client hints at past violence but says they cannot discuss details. What response best supports care?
options: We can discuss what helps you feel safe without requiring details.
We should complete the full history before deciding what support fits.
We can ask your partner to explain the parts you cannot discuss.
We should pause every assessment topic until you can tell the full story.
why: Safety supports and accommodations do not require a detailed trauma narrative.
Requiring full disclosure before support can undermine control and trust.
Seeking a partner's account may compromise privacy or safety.
Relevant care can continue with sensitive pacing and the client's consent.
takeaway: Support current safety needs without forcing trauma narration.
learningObjective: Support current safety needs without forcing trauma narration.

title: A trauma trigger in the environment
stem: A client becomes distressed when a door is closed during care and asks to keep it partly open. Privacy can still be maintained. What should the nurse do?
options: Insist on the usual door position
Ask for proof of the trauma history
Cancel the assessment automatically
Accommodate the preference and review other useful supports
why: Routine should not override a feasible individualized accommodation.
Trauma-informed care does not require proof of past events.
Care may proceed with acceptable adaptation.
A feasible choice can reduce distress and support participation.
takeaway: Accommodate safe environmental preferences that reduce trauma-related distress.
learningObjective: Accommodate safe environmental preferences that reduce trauma-related distress.

title: Avoiding retraumatization
stem: Which nursing practices reduce the risk of retraumatization? Select all that apply.
options: Explain the purpose of sensitive questions
Ask permission before physical contact
Use surprise to prevent anticipatory anxiety
Maintain predictable communication about changes
why: Knowing the purpose supports informed participation.
Permission supports bodily autonomy and control.
Unexpected actions may recreate loss of control.
Predictability reduces uncertainty and supports trust.
takeaway: Use consent and predictable communication throughout trauma-informed care.
learningObjective: Use consent and predictable communication throughout trauma-informed care.

title: Dissociation during an interview
stem: A client becomes distant, stares and says the room feels unreal during trauma discussion. What should the nurse do first?
options: Continue probing to obtain a complete history
Pause, assess immediate needs and use agreed grounding strategies
Interpret the behaviour as deliberate avoidance
Ask several staff to question the client simultaneously
why: Continued probing may intensify disconnection and distress.
Pausing and grounding support present orientation and safety.
Assumed motivation can lead to an unhelpful response.
Multiple questioners may increase overload.
takeaway: Pause trauma exploration when dissociation interferes with engagement.
learningObjective: Pause trauma exploration when dissociation interferes with engagement.

title: Recovery after a frightening event
stem: A client recently witnessed a serious collision and reports distress but has support and remains safe. What is the best initial nursing approach?
options: Require immediate detailed group retelling
Predict that post-traumatic stress disorder is inevitable
Assess practical needs, supports, symptoms and follow-up preferences
Advise avoiding all reminders permanently
why: Forced retelling is not a universal immediate support requirement.
Distress after an event does not establish a future diagnosis.
A needs-based approach supports coping without unsupported predictions.
Broad avoidance may restrict recovery and daily function.
takeaway: Provide needs-based support after trauma without forcing detailed retelling.
learningObjective: Provide needs-based support after trauma without forcing detailed retelling.

title: Trauma care and client control
stem: A client requests a different examiner for an intimate assessment because the current arrangement feels unsafe. No emergency exists. What should the nurse do?
options: Explore feasible alternatives and coordinate care with the client's agreement
Explain that the request proves unwillingness to receive care
Proceed because the assessment was ordered
Ask relatives to persuade the client to accept the examiner
why: Feasible alternatives preserve access while respecting control and consent.
A specific request does not equal refusal of all care.
An order does not eliminate consent requirements.
Persuasion may undermine the client's expressed safety needs.
takeaway: Seek feasible examination arrangements that support client control.
learningObjective: Seek feasible examination arrangements that support client control.

title: Evaluating trauma-informed care
stem: Which client statement best indicates that trauma-informed changes are helping?
options: 'I can describe every detail of the trauma now.'
'I no longer need any preferences respected.'
'The nurse decides when I should stop feeling afraid.'
'I know what will happen and can ask staff to pause.'
why: Detailed disclosure is not required to demonstrate safer care.
Continuing preferences is compatible with progress.
Emotional recovery is not determined by staff instruction.
Predictability and usable control are meaningful trauma-informed outcomes.
takeaway: Evaluate trauma-informed care through perceived safety, predictability and control.
learningObjective: Evaluate trauma-informed care through perceived safety, predictability and control.

title: Supporting a trusted companion
stem: A trauma survivor wants a friend present during education but not during examination. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Clarify the client's desired boundaries
Arrange the companion's involvement accordingly
Assume permission for teaching includes permission for examination
Recheck preferences if circumstances change
why: Specific boundaries clarify meaningful consent for involvement.
Respecting the distinction supports control and privacy.
Consent for one context does not automatically extend to another.
Preferences may change and should remain open to review.
takeaway: Treat support-person involvement as specific and revisable.
learningObjective: Treat support-person involvement as specific and revisable.

title: Depression hidden by physical complaints
stem: An older adult reports fatigue, poor concentration and loss of interest after medical causes begin being assessed. They deny feeling 'sad.' What should the nurse do?
options: Exclude depression because sadness is denied
Assess mood, pleasure, function and safety using accessible language
Attribute the changes solely to aging
Defer psychosocial assessment until every investigation is complete
why: Depression may present through somatic and functional complaints.
Broader questioning can identify distress not described as sadness.
Age alone does not explain a new functional decline.
Physical and psychosocial assessments can proceed together.
takeaway: Assess depression through function and interest as well as reported sadness.
learningObjective: Assess depression through function and interest as well as reported sadness.

title: Small tasks during severe depression
stem: A depressed client finds showering overwhelming but agrees to work on self-care. What plan is most appropriate?
options: Require all morning care without assistance
Wait for motivation before offering support
Break the task into manageable steps with graded assistance
Compare performance with a more independent client
why: An excessive initial demand may reinforce failure and withdrawal.
Support can help initiate activity before motivation improves.
Small achievable steps support function and evaluation.
Comparison may intensify shame rather than promote participation.
takeaway: Support depressed clients with manageable activities and graded assistance.
learningObjective: Support depressed clients with manageable activities and graded assistance.

title: Responding to worthlessness
stem: A client with depression says, 'I am useless because I cannot work.' What response best supports exploration?
options: 'Work seems closely tied to how you see your worth; tell me more.'
'You are useful, so that thought is wrong.'
'Other people have worse limitations.'
'You should find a new job immediately.'
why: Reflection explores meaning without arguing with the client.
Direct contradiction may not address the underlying belief.
Comparison can invalidate the client's distress.
Advice is premature before assessing capacity and concerns.
takeaway: Explore self-worth beliefs without relying on contradiction or comparison.
learningObjective: Explore self-worth beliefs without relying on contradiction or comparison.

title: Behavioural activation planning
stem: A client with depression has stopped enjoyable activities and agrees to try one small action. Which plan is best?
options: Schedule a full day of social events
Wait until every depressive symptom resolves
Choose the nurse's favourite activity for the client
Select a brief valued activity and review mood and function afterward
why: An overloaded plan may exceed current energy and concentration.
Waiting can prolong avoidance and inactivity.
Personal relevance matters for engagement.
A manageable meaningful action permits supported activity and evaluation.
takeaway: Use brief personally meaningful activities in a coordinated depression plan.
learningObjective: Use brief personally meaningful activities in a coordinated depression plan.

title: Assessing depressive impairment
stem: Which findings contribute to assessment of a possible depressive episode? Select all that apply.
options: Loss of pleasure in previously valued activities
Sustained changes in sleep and daily function
One isolated preference for quiet time
Persistent feelings of worthlessness
why: Loss of interest is a relevant depressive symptom.
Sustained changes help establish impact and pattern.
A single preference does not establish a depressive syndrome.
Worthlessness warrants further mood and safety assessment.
takeaway: Assess sustained symptom patterns and functional impact in depression.
learningObjective: Assess sustained symptom patterns and functional impact in depression.

title: Depression and decision load
stem: A client with depression becomes distressed when offered six breakfast choices. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the client to decide faster
Offer two acceptable choices and allow response time
Choose every future meal without consultation
Remove breakfast until a decision is made
why: Pressure can worsen distress when concentration is impaired.
Limited choices support autonomy with lower cognitive demand.
Permanent takeover unnecessarily removes participation.
Withholding nutrition does not address impaired decision-making.
takeaway: Reduce decision complexity while preserving choice during depression.
learningObjective: Reduce decision complexity while preserving choice during depression.

title: Family interpretation of depression
stem: A spouse says, 'If they cared about us, they would get out of bed.' What is the best response?
options: Agree that family pressure is the main treatment
Advise withdrawing all support
Explain how depression affects energy and discuss supportive expectations
Promise recovery as soon as the client tries harder
why: Blame does not address illness-related impairment.
Support withdrawal may increase isolation and unmet needs.
Education can reduce blame while supporting realistic participation.
Effort alone does not determine recovery timing.
takeaway: Explain depressive impairment without removing all expectations for supported activity.
learningObjective: Explain depressive impairment without removing all expectations for supported activity.

title: Evaluating depression recovery
stem: Which finding best supports improved functioning in a depressed client?
options: Resuming a chosen daily task with less assistance
Memorizing the names of mood disorders
Agreeing with every nurse suggestion
Smiling briefly during a visitor's joke
why: Sustained participation reflects meaningful functional improvement.
Knowledge alone does not establish recovery.
Compliance may not reflect improved mood or ability.
A single smile does not describe the overall course.
takeaway: Evaluate depression using sustained function and symptom patterns.
learningObjective: Evaluate depression using sustained function and symptom patterns.

title: Depression screening result
stem: A client has an elevated depression screening score but has not had a diagnostic assessment. What should the nurse explain?
options: The score proves a specific psychiatric diagnosis
The score determines treatment without clinical discussion
A low score on another day would exclude all concern
The result indicates a need for further assessment, including safety
why: Screening supports detection rather than independently confirming diagnosis.
Treatment requires clinical context and shared assessment.
Symptoms and risk can vary and need contextual interpretation.
Further review clarifies symptoms, function, contributors and risk.
takeaway: Use depression screening as a route to clinical assessment.
learningObjective: Use depression screening as a route to clinical assessment.

title: Supporting depression follow-up
stem: Which discharge preparations support continuity for a client recovering from depression? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm a follow-up appointment and access plan
Review early worsening signs and whom to contact
End follow-up once sleep improves for one night
Identify practical support for agreed daily routines
why: A usable appointment plan reduces transition gaps.
Recognition and contacts support timely response to recurrence.
One improved symptom does not establish sustained recovery.
Practical support can help maintain function during recovery.
takeaway: Plan depression follow-up around access, recurrence signs and daily supports.
learningObjective: Plan depression follow-up around access, recurrence signs and daily supports.

title: Postpartum mood assessment
stem: At six weeks postpartum, a client reports persistent hopelessness, poor functioning and inability to enjoy anything. What should the nurse do?
options: Normalize the symptoms as expected adjustment without further questions
Arrange mental-health assessment and assess immediate safety
Focus only on the infant's feeding schedule
Wait until the infant sleeps through the night
why: Persistent impairment requires assessment rather than routine reassurance.
Mood symptoms and safety need timely evaluation and support.
Feeding review alone does not address the client's distress.
Waiting may delay treatment of a significant condition.
takeaway: Assess persistent postpartum mood symptoms that impair functioning.
learningObjective: Assess persistent postpartum mood symptoms that impair functioning.

title: Postpartum psychosis warning
stem: A client one week postpartum has barely slept and believes the infant is controlled by a dangerous force. What is the priority?
options: Schedule routine counselling next month
Ask the family to debate the belief
Arrange emergency assessment and immediate parent-infant safety support
Encourage independent infant care to build confidence
why: Possible postpartum psychosis requires urgent rather than routine review.
Argument does not reliably restore reality testing or safety.
Acute psychotic symptoms after birth can pose serious immediate risks.
Independent care is inappropriate until safety is assessed.
takeaway: Treat new postpartum psychosis as an emergency.
learningObjective: Treat new postpartum psychosis as an emergency.

title: Adolescent irritability and withdrawal
stem: A teenager has become persistently irritable, withdrawn and less successful at school. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Assess mood, functioning, substance use and safety privately as appropriate
Assume ordinary adolescence explains the entire change
Focus only on enforcing homework rules
Wait for the teenager to describe sadness spontaneously
why: Depression in youth may present through irritability and functional change.
Persistent changes warrant assessment rather than developmental dismissal.
Rules alone do not evaluate potential health concerns.
The young person may not use adult descriptions of low mood.
takeaway: Include depression in assessment of sustained adolescent irritability and decline.
learningObjective: Include depression in assessment of sustained adolescent irritability and decline.

title: Depression with physical illness
stem: A client recovering from a stroke reports hopelessness and stops rehabilitation. What should the nurse do?
options: Assume rehabilitation refusal is a fixed preference
Discuss only muscle strength goals
Delay mood assessment until physical recovery is complete
Assess depressive symptoms and barriers while preserving achievable rehabilitation goals
why: Withdrawal may reflect treatable mood or practical difficulties.
Physical goals alone may miss the reason for disengagement.
Mood difficulties can interfere with recovery and deserve timely assessment.
Integrated assessment addresses participation and emotional needs together.
takeaway: Assess mood when hopelessness interferes with physical rehabilitation.
learningObjective: Assess mood when hopelessness interferes with physical rehabilitation.

title: Monitoring change during treatment
stem: Which changes during depression treatment require prompt reassessment? Select all that apply.
options: New agitation with suicidal thoughts
Markedly reduced need for sleep with unusual impulsivity
A gradual return to a valued routine
New inability to meet basic intake needs
why: Agitation with suicidality can increase immediate risk.
A possible mood switch needs timely clinical review.
Gradual functional improvement is an expected positive outcome.
Inadequate intake can create urgent physical consequences.
takeaway: Reassess new risk, activation or physical compromise during mood treatment.
learningObjective: Reassess new risk, activation or physical compromise during mood treatment.

title: Sudden calm after suicidal distress
stem: A client recently expressed intense suicidal thoughts and now appears unexpectedly calm after giving away possessions. What should the nurse do?
options: Reduce observation because the mood appears better
Reassess suicide risk promptly and maintain current precautions pending review
Focus only on the donated items' value
Wait for the client to volunteer a new concern
why: Apparent calm does not establish safety and can accompany a decision to act.
The behavioural change requires direct reassessment before reducing protection.
Monetary value is less relevant than the meaning of giving belongings away.
Risk assessment should respond actively to concerning changes.
takeaway: Reassess suicide risk when behaviour changes despite apparent mood improvement.
learningObjective: Reassess suicide risk when behaviour changes despite apparent mood improvement.

title: A negative answer with concerning collateral
stem: A client denies suicidal thoughts, but a family member reports recent farewell messages. What is the best response?
options: Disregard the family because the client denied risk
Accept the messages as proof of a specific plan without assessment
Explore the discrepancy and assess risk using all available information
Ask the family to decide discharge readiness
why: Denial alone does not resolve credible concerning information.
Collateral information requires assessment rather than unsupported conclusions.
Combining sources supports a fuller safety evaluation.
Discharge judgment requires the clinical team and applicable processes.
takeaway: Integrate collateral information into suicide-risk assessment.
learningObjective: Integrate collateral information into suicide-risk assessment.

title: Limits of a safety promise
stem: A client at suicide risk promises, 'I will not hurt myself.' What should the nurse conclude?
options: The promise does not replace assessment, observation or a safety plan
Observation can end immediately
A written version guarantees safety
Further questions would invalidate the promise
why: A promise cannot reliably establish risk level or substitute for protection.
Precaution changes require reassessment and appropriate clinical decisions.
Signing does not transform a promise into a guarantee.
Direct ongoing assessment remains necessary and supportive.
takeaway: Do not use a no-harm promise as a substitute for suicide assessment.
learningObjective: Do not use a no-harm promise as a substitute for suicide assessment.

title: Meaningful protective factors
stem: A client says caring for a pet helps them resist suicidal thoughts but also reports an active plan. What should the nurse recognize?
options: A protective relationship eliminates current risk
Only the plan matters and the pet is irrelevant
Discussing the pet replaces assessment of intent
The protective factor is useful but does not cancel the active risk
why: Protective factors do not guarantee safety when acute risks remain.
Protective connections may contribute to a future safety plan.
Intent and access still require direct assessment.
Both risk and protective information belong in the clinical formulation.
takeaway: Assess protective factors without treating them as guarantees against suicide.
learningObjective: Assess protective factors without treating them as guarantees against suicide.

title: Elements of a safety plan
stem: Which components belong in a collaborative suicide safety plan? Select all that apply.
options: Personal warning signs and coping actions
People and services the client can contact
A promise that no crisis will recur
Steps to reduce access to means of self-harm
why: Recognizable cues and coping steps support early action.
Practical contacts provide escalating sources of help.
Recurrence cannot be ruled out by agreement.
Reducing access is an important preventive component.
takeaway: Build a practical safety plan with warning signs, coping, contacts and means safety.
learningObjective: Build a practical safety plan with warning signs, coping, contacts and means safety.

title: Practising a crisis plan
stem: A client can name their safety-plan contacts but says they would not know what to say during distress. What should the nurse do?
options: Add more phone numbers without discussion
Rehearse a brief help-seeking message with the client
Remove contacts the client feels nervous about using
Assume written numbers alone are sufficient
why: More numbers do not address the communication barrier.
Rehearsal makes the plan easier to use during crisis.
Nervousness may be addressed rather than automatically eliminating support.
Knowing a number does not establish ability to use it.
takeaway: Practise how to request help as part of safety planning.
learningObjective: Practise how to request help as part of safety planning.

title: Confidentiality and acute risk
stem: A client discloses an imminent self-harm plan but asks the nurse to tell nobody. What should the nurse explain?
options: Everything must remain secret if the client requests it
Disclosure will be made to every staff member in the facility
Necessary people must be involved to protect safety, with the client informed as possible
Only a family member can authorize a safety response
why: Confidentiality is not absolute when immediate safety is threatened.
Information should be shared for legitimate safety needs, not indiscriminately.
Transparent limited sharing supports safety and trust.
Emergency safety actions do not depend solely on family authorization.
takeaway: Explain necessary safety-related sharing without promising absolute secrecy.
learningObjective: Explain necessary safety-related sharing without promising absolute secrecy.

title: Supervision during an urgent assessment
stem: A client under ordered continuous observation for acute suicide risk needs transfer for assessment. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Maintain the prescribed observation through a clear supervised handoff
Send the client ahead while staff arrange paperwork
Substitute a family visit for observation without review
Reduce supervision because the receiving unit is secure
why: Transitions must preserve the established protective observation level.
Unsupervised gaps undermine the purpose of continuous observation.
Family presence does not automatically replace clinical requirements.
Unit design alone does not authorize a precaution change.
takeaway: Maintain suicide precautions across transitions until appropriately reassessed.
learningObjective: Maintain suicide precautions across transitions until appropriately reassessed.

title: Asking about access to means
stem: A client reports intermittent suicidal thoughts without describing a method. Why should the nurse ask about access to potentially harmful items?
options: To determine whether the client is being truthful by surprise
To complete a form without discussing the answer
To decide whether emotional support is unnecessary
To understand risk and plan practical steps to reduce access
why: The purpose is assessment and safety, not catching the client out.
Responses need clinical interpretation and follow-through.
Means assessment complements rather than replaces emotional support.
Available means influence immediate safety planning.
takeaway: Assess access to means to guide concrete protective actions.
learningObjective: Assess access to means to guide concrete protective actions.

title: Evaluating a proposed discharge safety plan
stem: Which findings indicate that a safety plan needs revision before it can be relied upon? Select all that apply.
options: The only listed contact is unreachable overnight
The client cannot access the promised follow-up service
The client identifies a personal early warning sign
A support person agreed to a role without knowing what it involves
why: An unavailable contact creates a predictable access gap.
A plan depending on inaccessible care is not operational.
Recognizing a warning sign supports plan usefulness.
Support roles need clear agreement and practical understanding.
takeaway: Verify that safety-plan resources are reachable and understood.
learningObjective: Verify that safety-plan resources are reachable and understood.

title: Self-injury without stated suicidal intent
stem: A client reports cutting to relieve distress and denies wanting to die. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess injuries, function of self-injury and suicide risk
Assume suicide risk is absent because intent is denied
Focus only on stopping the behaviour through criticism
Delay wound assessment until counselling is completed
why: Physical care and direct risk assessment are both necessary.
Nonsuicidal intent does not eliminate concurrent or future suicide risk.
Criticism may increase shame and reduce disclosure.
Injuries require timely assessment regardless of behavioural purpose.
takeaway: Assess both physical injury and suicide risk after self-injury.
learningObjective: Assess both physical injury and suicide risk after self-injury.

title: Responding after self-injury disclosure
stem: After wounds are assessed, a client says, 'You must think I am attention-seeking.' What response is most therapeutic?
options: 'You should have used a different method.'
'I want to understand the distress and what helps you stay safe.'
'We should avoid discussing the behaviour again.'
'Your family can decide whether the distress is real.'
why: Method comparison is not a therapeutic response to distress.
Nonjudgmental exploration supports trust and safer coping.
Avoidance prevents assessment of the behaviour's function.
The client's distress does not require family validation.
takeaway: Respond to self-injury with nonjudgmental assessment of distress and safety.
learningObjective: Respond to self-injury with nonjudgmental assessment of distress and safety.

title: Choosing safer coping alternatives
stem: A client who self-injures identifies rising tension before episodes. What should the nurse do within the treatment plan?
options: Recommend suppressing every feeling without support
Select a coping method without asking preferences
Rehearse agreed noninjurious strategies at the early-tension stage
Wait until another injury before discussing coping
why: Suppression alone may not provide effective regulation.
Strategies need to be acceptable and feasible for the client.
Early practice links identifiable cues with safer responses.
Waiting misses an opportunity for prevention.
takeaway: Connect early self-harm cues with rehearsed noninjurious coping.
learningObjective: Connect early self-harm cues with rehearsed noninjurious coping.

title: Digital messages suggesting risk
stem: A client shows farewell messages they drafted but did not send and says they feel embarrassed. What is the best response?
options: Explore intent, timing, current thoughts and safety needs directly
Reassure solely because the messages were not sent
Focus on deleting the messages before assessment
Ask whether the writing is grammatically clear
why: Preparatory communication can indicate risk and warrants direct assessment.
Lack of sending does not establish absence of intent.
Deletion does not evaluate or resolve the underlying risk.
Editing details are unrelated to immediate safety needs.
takeaway: Assess the meaning of preparatory or farewell communication.
learningObjective: Assess the meaning of preparatory or farewell communication.

title: A support person's role
stem: A client wants a sibling involved in a suicide safety plan. What should the nurse clarify?
options: That the sibling guarantees no future crisis
That professional follow-up is no longer needed
That the sibling should conceal every concern from clinicians
Agreed warning signs, practical actions and emergency contact routes
why: No support person can guarantee future safety.
Family support complements rather than replaces professional care.
Relevant safety concerns may require timely clinical communication.
Specific shared responsibilities make involvement useful and realistic.
takeaway: Define concrete support roles without transferring all responsibility to family.
learningObjective: Define concrete support roles without transferring all responsibility to family.

title: Crisis resources in Canada
stem: Which statements about a Canadian client's crisis-contact plan are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Call or text 9-8-8 for suicide crisis support
Use emergency services when immediate safety is at risk
Wait for office hours before contacting any service
Keep contact methods in a format the client can access
why: Canada's 9-8-8 service offers around-the-clock crisis support.
Immediate danger requires an emergency response.
Crisis needs may occur outside routine service hours.
Usability matters when concentration and coping are impaired.
takeaway: Distinguish crisis support from emergency response and make contacts accessible.
learningObjective: Distinguish crisis support from emergency response and make contacts accessible.

title: Suicide risk after an acute loss
stem: A client lost housing yesterday, is intoxicated and says nothing matters. What should guide the nurse's response?
options: Wait for sobriety before providing any safety measures
Assess immediate safety and physical needs while arranging continued reassessment
Attribute the statement solely to alcohol
Focus only on housing paperwork until the client is calmer
why: Protective care should not be delayed while capacity to participate improves.
Intoxication and acute stress require immediate care plus reassessment over time.
Alcohol does not make suicidal statements clinically irrelevant.
Practical needs matter but do not replace immediate safety assessment.
takeaway: Provide immediate safety care when intoxication limits a complete suicide assessment.
learningObjective: Provide immediate safety care when intoxication limits a complete suicide assessment.

title: Risk documentation
stem: After a suicide-risk assessment, which documentation is most useful?
options: 'Client is safe' without supporting information
'Attention-seeking' as the main description
Relevant statements, observed cues, assessment findings and protective actions
Only the total score from a screening form
why: A broad label does not communicate evidence or limits.
A judgmental label obscures the actual clinical findings.
Specific evidence and actions support continuity and reassessment.
A score alone omits context and clinical judgment.
takeaway: Document suicide-risk evidence and the actions taken.
learningObjective: Document suicide-risk evidence and the actions taken.

title: Emerging mania
stem: A client with bipolar disorder has slept very little for three nights, feels unusually energetic and is spending impulsively. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange prompt clinical review of possible mood escalation
Praise improved energy without further assessment
Advise making major purchases while confidence is high
Wait for overt psychosis before contacting the team
why: Reduced sleep with impulsivity may signal a developing manic episode.
Increased energy can represent deterioration rather than recovery.
Major decisions may be impaired by mood elevation.
Earlier recognition allows intervention before more severe disruption.
takeaway: Recognize reduced sleep and impulsivity as possible early mania.
learningObjective: Recognize reduced sleep and impulsivity as possible early mania.

title: Nutrition during mania
stem: A client experiencing mania paces continuously and leaves meals after a few bites. Which approach best supports intake?
options: Require sitting through a lengthy group meal
Focus exclusively on discussing food choices
Remove snacks to increase hunger at meals
Offer manageable nutritious foods and fluids with brief support
why: A long seated meal may exceed current concentration and activity tolerance.
Discussion alone does not improve actual intake.
Removing opportunities may worsen inadequate nutrition.
Accessible small offerings can fit the client's current behaviour.
takeaway: Adapt nutrition support to the activity and attention patterns of mania.
learningObjective: Adapt nutrition support to the activity and attention patterns of mania.

title: Supporting sleep in mania
stem: Which nursing actions fit a coordinated plan for a client with acute mania? Select all that apply.
options: Reduce unnecessary evening stimulation
Monitor sleep and rest patterns
Encourage late-night competitive activities to tire the client
Provide predictable brief interactions
why: Lower stimulation supports an environment more compatible with rest.
Sleep trends inform severity and treatment response.
Competition and stimulation may intensify activation.
Predictable concise contact reduces overload and conflict.
takeaway: Support rest through environmental adaptation and monitoring during mania.
learningObjective: Support rest through environmental adaptation and monitoring during mania.

title: Limit setting during mania
stem: A client with mania repeatedly enters other clients' rooms. What is the best nursing response?
options: Explain every policy in a lengthy lecture
State a brief clear boundary and redirect to an appropriate space
Ignore the behaviour until someone complains
Negotiate different privacy rules each time
why: Lengthy explanations may exceed current attention and escalate frustration.
Clear consistent limits protect others while giving a usable alternative.
Waiting permits continued intrusion and possible conflict.
Variable rules reduce predictability and effectiveness.
takeaway: Use brief consistent boundaries with a concrete alternative during mania.
learningObjective: Use brief consistent boundaries with a concrete alternative during mania.

title: Impulsive financial decisions
stem: A hospitalized client with mania wants to make a large nonurgent purchase during marked distractibility. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete the transaction to preserve rapport
Decide the client's finances independently
Encourage postponement and involve the treatment team in assessing decision support needs
Ask another client to advise on the investment
why: Facilitating a major decision during impairment can increase harm.
Nurses do not automatically gain financial decision authority.
A pause and appropriate assessment protect autonomy and reduce impulsive harm.
Another client's opinion does not establish appropriate support.
takeaway: Address impulsive high-impact decisions through delay and appropriate assessment.
learningObjective: Address impulsive high-impact decisions through delay and appropriate assessment.

title: Communication with pressured speech
stem: A client with mania speaks rapidly and changes topics before a question is completed. What approach is best?
options: Use brief concrete statements and gently return to the immediate topic
Match the client's speech speed and volume
Ask several questions together to save time
Explore multiple abstract themes simultaneously
why: Concise redirection supports comprehension despite distractibility.
Mirroring intensity may increase stimulation.
Multiple questions add cognitive load.
Abstract branching discussion may worsen disorganization.
takeaway: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.
learningObjective: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.

title: Family plan for bipolar recurrence
stem: A client agrees to involve family in relapse prevention. What information is most useful?
options: A prediction that relapse cannot recur with support
A rule that every happy mood requires emergency care
A list of unrelated diagnostic terms
The client's early changes, agreed contacts and preferred support actions
why: Support reduces risk but cannot guarantee no recurrence.
Normal happiness is not equivalent to mania.
Vocabulary alone does not guide practical action.
Individualized early cues and responses make the plan actionable.
takeaway: Build bipolar relapse plans around the client's own early warning pattern.
learningObjective: Build bipolar relapse plans around the client's own early warning pattern.

title: Evaluating mania improvement
stem: Which findings suggest improvement in a client treated for mania? Select all that apply.
options: Longer sustained sleep periods
Better ability to remain with a simple task
Increased impulsive spending plans
Improved food and fluid intake
why: Restoring sleep can indicate reduced activation.
Improved attention supports meaningful functional recovery.
Growing impulsivity suggests continuing impaired judgment.
Improved intake addresses a common physical consequence of mania.
takeaway: Evaluate manic recovery through sleep, attention, judgment and basic needs.
learningObjective: Evaluate manic recovery through sleep, attention, judgment and basic needs.

title: Mood tracking for bipolar disorder
stem: A stable client wants to recognize recurrence earlier. Which tracking approach is most useful?
options: Record sleep, mood, activity and relevant triggers over time
Record only days that feel unusually positive
Use weight as the sole marker of mood stability
Ask family to infer the pattern without the client's input
why: Multiple daily patterns can reveal individualized early changes.
Selective entries may obscure depressive or mixed changes.
Weight alone does not describe mood recurrence.
The client's own experience is an important part of tracking.
takeaway: Track mood alongside sleep, activity and context in bipolar care.
learningObjective: Track mood alongside sleep, activity and context in bipolar care.

title: Feeling well and treatment continuation
stem: A stable client with bipolar disorder wants to stop follow-up because they feel well. What response best supports informed care?
options: Agree that follow-up is only useful during crises
Discuss maintenance goals and review concerns with the treating team
Tell the client recurrence is certain tomorrow
Focus only on past hospital costs
why: Maintenance care may support sustained stability and early recognition.
Collaborative review addresses preferences without abrupt unsupported changes.
An exact prediction is unjustified and fear-based.
Cost alone does not address the client's treatment question.
takeaway: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.
learningObjective: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.

title: Depressive and activated symptoms together
stem: A client reports hopelessness while pacing, sleeping little and describing racing thoughts. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Assume increased energy means low suicide risk
Wait for a clearly elevated mood before review
Assess safety promptly and report the mixed symptom pattern
Focus only on bedtime routines
why: Energy and agitation can coexist with serious suicidal distress.
Clinically important activation need not appear as cheerful mood.
The combined pattern may create significant risk and needs clinical review.
Sleep advice alone is insufficient for this presentation.
takeaway: Escalate hopelessness accompanied by activation or agitation.
learningObjective: Escalate hopelessness accompanied by activation or agitation.

title: Distinguishing reduced need from insomnia
stem: A client sleeps two hours and says they feel fully rested, unusually powerful and ready for major projects. What is most concerning?
options: Reduced sleep need with activation and grandiosity
The bedtime differs from the nurse's routine
The client prefers morning activity
The client recalls a vivid dream
why: The combined pattern suggests possible manic escalation requiring assessment.
Schedule differences alone do not establish a disorder.
Activity preference alone is not an acute warning sign.
Dream recall does not explain the activation pattern.
takeaway: Assess reduced sleep need together with energy and judgment changes.
learningObjective: Assess reduced sleep need together with energy and judgment changes.

title: Protecting dignity during disinhibition
stem: A client with mania makes sexual comments toward peers. What should the nurse do?
options: Discuss the behaviour publicly to deter repetition
Ignore comments because they reflect illness
Encourage peers to confront the client as a group
Set respectful limits, redirect and assess the care plan
why: Public humiliation can escalate distress and damage dignity.
Illness does not remove the need to protect others' boundaries.
Group confrontation may intensify conflict.
Clear respectful intervention supports safety without shaming.
takeaway: Address disinhibition with dignity, limits and coordinated reassessment.
learningObjective: Address disinhibition with dignity, limits and coordinated reassessment.

title: Selecting manageable activities
stem: Which activities may fit a client whose mania is improving but who remains distractible? Select all that apply.
options: Brief simple tasks with staff support
Quiet noncompetitive activity with limited choices
A complex competitive tournament with many rules
Planned rest opportunities between activities
why: Simple supported tasks match limited sustained attention.
Lower stimulation reduces overload and competition-related escalation.
Complex competition may exceed attention and increase activation.
Rest opportunities support recovery from prolonged activation.
takeaway: Match activity complexity and stimulation to current manic recovery.
learningObjective: Match activity complexity and stimulation to current manic recovery.

title: Food-related suspiciousness
stem: A client with psychosis refuses meals because they fear tampering. They will accept intact packaged food. What is the best immediate nursing approach?
options: Argue that staff would never tamper with food
Offer acceptable sealed food while assessing intake and the belief's effect
Agree that ordinary meals are contaminated
Delay nutrition until the belief disappears
why: Argument may increase mistrust without improving intake.
An acceptable option supports nutrition without endorsing the belief.
Confirming contamination reinforces the delusional interpretation.
Waiting can worsen physical needs while symptoms persist.
takeaway: Support basic needs without validating a delusion.
learningObjective: Support basic needs without validating a delusion.

title: Thought blocking in conversation
stem: A client suddenly stops speaking mid-sentence and appears unable to continue. What should the nurse do?
options: Supply the likely ending immediately
Change topics several times to stimulate speech
Allow time and gently ask whether the client wants to continue
Interpret the pause as agreement with the nurse
why: Supplying content may distort the client's intended meaning.
Rapid topic changes add cognitive demands.
A patient pause supports communication without imposing an explanation.
Silence does not establish agreement.
takeaway: Allow time and clarify sudden interruptions in thought.
learningObjective: Allow time and clarify sudden interruptions in thought.

title: Responding to unusual word meanings
stem: A client uses a word the nurse does not understand while describing distress. What is the best response?
options: Ask what that word means to the client
Pretend to understand to maintain rapport
Correct the vocabulary before assessing distress
Ask another client to translate the meaning
why: Clarification supports accurate understanding of the experience.
Pretending can lead to inaccurate assessment and care.
Language correction may distract from the clinical meaning.
Another client's interpretation cannot reliably replace clarification.
takeaway: Clarify unfamiliar language instead of assigning meaning.
learningObjective: Clarify unfamiliar language instead of assigning meaning.

title: Low initiation in schizophrenia
stem: A stable client with schizophrenia rarely begins hygiene tasks but participates when offered one-step prompts. What should the nurse do?
options: Label the client unwilling to cooperate
Withdraw prompts to test motivation
Provide long lists of tasks each morning
Use consistent manageable prompts and assess other contributors
why: Reduced initiation may reflect symptoms rather than deliberate refusal.
Removing effective support may worsen function.
Long lists may exceed attention or planning ability.
Structured support addresses function while considering depression or adverse effects.
takeaway: Support reduced initiation without assuming deliberate noncooperation.
learningObjective: Support reduced initiation without assuming deliberate noncooperation.

title: Assessing hallucination impact
stem: A client reports hearing voices. Which questions help determine the care needed? Select all that apply.
options: 'What do the voices say?'
'Do they tell you to do something?'
'Would proving they are unreal end this discussion?'
'How do they affect what you do?'
'Are you definitely ignoring them successfully?'
why: Content helps identify distress and safety implications.
Commands require further risk assessment.
Debate does not assess impact or coping.
Behavioural effects reveal functional and safety needs.
A leading assumption can conceal difficulty resisting voices.
takeaway: Assess hallucination content, commands and behavioural effects.
learningObjective: Assess hallucination content, commands and behavioural effects.

title: Coping with noncommand voices
stem: A client hears distressing noncommand voices and identifies quiet music as helpful. What should the nurse do?
options: Require the same strategy for every client
Support the preferred strategy and reassess distress and safety
Tell the client to stop mentioning voices
Increase background sound regardless of preference
why: Coping responses differ among clients.
An effective chosen strategy can be integrated with ongoing assessment.
Suppressing disclosure undermines assessment and support.
More noise may increase distress rather than reduce it.
takeaway: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.
learningObjective: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.

title: Psychosis and physical symptoms
stem: A client with chronic schizophrenia reports new abdominal pain and vomiting. What is the appropriate nursing response?
options: Attribute the report to delusional thinking
Delay assessment until the psychiatric review
Assess the physical symptoms and escalate findings appropriately
Ask whether hallucinations caused the pain before checking physical status
why: A psychiatric diagnosis does not exclude physical illness.
New symptoms may require timely medical evaluation.
Physical assessment prevents diagnostic overshadowing.
Symptom attribution should not delay basic clinical assessment.
takeaway: Investigate physical symptoms in clients with mental illness.
learningObjective: Investigate physical symptoms in clients with mental illness.

title: Distractibility during self-care teaching
stem: A client recovering from psychosis loses track during multistep instructions. What adaptation is best?
options: Teach one step at a time with practice
Repeat the full sequence more rapidly
Postpone every self-care activity until concentration is normal
Rely only on an extensive written manual
why: Single steps match current processing and allow feedback.
Faster delivery increases rather than reduces cognitive load.
Supported participation may be possible before full symptom resolution.
Lengthy reading may exceed the same cognitive capacity.
takeaway: Break self-care learning into manageable steps during psychosis recovery.
learningObjective: Break self-care learning into manageable steps during psychosis recovery.

title: Delusional fear of assessment
stem: A client believes a blood-pressure cuff can read thoughts and refuses it. No urgent measurement is needed. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply it quickly while the client is distracted
